title: Data structures, ADTs and algorithm analysis
kicker: ENCT 252 · Data Structure and Algorithms · Chapter 1
subtitle: Choose how to store data, and know how the cost of working with it grows.

sections.title: Why structure matters
sections.body: A data structure is a way of organising data so that the operations you need are cheap. An array gives instant access by index but costly insertion in the middle; a linked list inserts cheaply but finds slowly; a hash table finds almost instantly but keeps no order. An abstract data type (ADT) states what operations exist (stack: push, pop, peek) independent of how they are implemented (array or linked list).

choices.text: A specification of operations, independent of implementation.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: A stack can be built on an array or on a linked list without changing its users.

sections.title: Algorithm design techniques
sections.body: Recurring strategies: brute force (try everything), divide and conquer (split, solve, combine — merge sort), greedy (take the best local choice — Huffman), dynamic programming (remember sub-answers), backtracking (build and undo), branch and bound, randomised and recursive algorithms.

questions.prompt: Merge sort is an example of…

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: No local best choice is committed to.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It splits the array, sorts the halves, and merges.

sections.title: Growth rates and Big-O
sections.body:
We measure cost as a function of input size n and keep only the dominant term. Big-O is an upper bound (f = O(g) if f ≤ c·g for large n), Big-Omega a lower bound, Big-Theta both. Best, worst and average cases can differ: linear search is O(1) best, O(n) worst. Common orders, slowest-growing first: 1, log n, n, n log n, n², n³, 2ⁿ, n!.

Count real operations: bubble sort on 5 1 4 2 8 makes 9 comparisons and 4 swaps; merge sort makes 8 comparisons.

worked.why: Show 3n² + 5n + 20 = O(n²): choose c and n₀ with 3n² + 5n + 20 ≤ c·n² for n ≥ n₀.
For n ≥ 1: 5n ≤ 5n² and 20 ≤ 20n², so the sum is at most 28n².

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: For large n the n² term dominates; constants are dropped.

sections.title: Counting loops
sections.body: A single loop to n is O(n); nested loops to n are O(n²); a loop that doubles its counter (i *= 2) runs log₂ n times. Run the program and the DSA Lab counts the iterations.

questions.prompt: for (i = 1; i < n; i *= 2) runs how many times?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The counter doubles, so it needs log₂ n steps to reach n.

figures.caption: Figure 1.4.1 — Counting loops

problems.prompt: What is the complexity of two nested loops, each from 1 to n, with the inner body O(1)?

problems.answer: The counter halves each time: O(log n).

sections.title: Space complexity and trade-offs
sections.body: Space complexity counts the extra memory an algorithm needs. Merge sort needs O(n) extra space; heap sort and quick sort (average) sort in place. Often time can be bought with space — a lookup table or memoisation — and the reverse.

questions.prompt: Which sort uses O(1) extra space?

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• Pick the structure whose cheap operations match your workload.
  • Big-O keeps the dominant term: n² beats n log n beats n.
  • Measure by counting operations, not seconds.
